module_title: Choosing the Best Wheat and Barley Varieties

lessons.title: Understanding Wheat Classes: Bread, Biscuit, and Durum
lessons.body: Wheat is not just wheat. There are three main classes you need to know: bread wheat, biscuit wheat, and durum wheat. Each has different uses and growing requirements. Bread wheat is the most common. It has high protein and strong gluten, making it perfect for yeast breads. In Africa, bread wheat is grown in Ethiopia, Kenya, and South Africa. Varieties like 'Kakaba' in Ethiopia or 'Kenya Nyangumi' are popular. Bread wheat needs 400-600 mm of rainfall or irrigation. It takes 120-150 days to mature. Biscuit wheat, also called soft wheat, has weaker gluten. It is used for cakes, biscuits, and pastries. It yields well in cooler, wetter areas. In Kenya, 'Kenya Fahari' is a biscuit wheat. It matures in 110-130 days. Durum wheat is the hardest. It has very high protein and is used for pasta, couscous, and semolina. Durum thrives in hot, dry conditions. It is grown in Ethiopia, Morocco, and Algeria. 'Yerer' and 'Ude' are durum varieties in Ethiopia. Durum needs 300-500 mm of rainfall and 100-120 days to mature. When choosing a class, think about your market. If you sell to a bread bakery, grow bread wheat. If you supply a pasta factory, grow durum. If you sell to a biscuit company, grow biscuit wheat. Also check your local climate. Durum does best in dry heat. Bread wheat is more adaptable. Biscuit wheat needs cool, moist conditions. Always test a small plot before planting a whole field. Talk to other farmers and extension officers. They can tell you which class works best in your area. Remember, seed of the wrong class will not get a good price. So choose carefully from the start.

lessons.title: Barley Types: Two-Row, Six-Row, and Malting Barley
lessons.body: Barley comes in three main types: two-row, six-row, and malting barley. Two-row barley has two rows of seeds on each spike. The seeds are large and uniform. It is often used for food and feed. Two-row barley is popular in Ethiopia and Kenya. It yields well in highlands. Varieties like 'HB-42' and 'Sabini' are two-row. It matures in 90-120 days. Six-row barley has six rows of seeds. The seeds are smaller and less uniform. It is mainly used for animal feed. Six-row barley is grown in Egypt and Morocco. It tolerates poorer soils. Varieties like 'Giza 123' and 'ACSAD 176' are six-row. It matures in 80-110 days. Malting barley is a special type. It must have low protein and high starch. It is used to make beer and malt. Malting barley fetches a higher price. But it needs specific conditions. It requires cool, moist weather during grain filling. It also needs uniform maturity. In Africa, malting barley is grown in Ethiopia, Kenya, and South Africa. Varieties like 'Grace' and 'Maltings' are used. Malting barley must meet strict quality standards. The grains must be plump and even. They must have low nitrogen. If you grow malting barley, you must dry it properly. You also need a contract with a maltster. Without a buyer, malting barley is risky. For most smallholder farmers, two-row or six-row barley for feed or food is safer. They are easier to grow and have a ready local market. Choose based on your soil, rainfall, and market. If you have irrigation and a contract, try malting barley. If not, stick to feed barley. Always buy certified seed to ensure the type is true.

lessons.title: Drought-Tolerant and Disease-Resistant Varieties for Africa
lessons.body: Africa has unpredictable rainfall. Drought can wipe out your crop. That is why you need drought-tolerant varieties. These varieties have deep roots and can survive dry spells. They also mature early. For wheat, look for varieties like 'Danda'a' in Ethiopia. It matures in 85-95 days and yields well with little water. 'Kingbird' is another drought-tolerant wheat in Kenya. It can produce 2-3 tonnes per hectare with only 300 mm of rain. For barley, 'Mari' and 'Shage' in Ethiopia are drought-tolerant. They mature in 80-90 days. 'Giza 123' in Egypt is also drought-tolerant. Disease is another big problem. Rusts, smuts, and bunts can destroy your crop. Disease-resistant varieties are your best defense. For wheat, look for resistance to stem rust, yellow rust, and leaf rust. In Ethiopia, 'Kakaba' is resistant to stem rust. 'Hidase' is resistant to yellow rust. In Kenya, 'Kenya Tai' is resistant to both. For barley, look for resistance to barley yellow dwarf virus and net blotch. 'HB-42' is resistant to net blotch. 'Sabini' is resistant to yellow dwarf. When you buy seed, ask for the resistance profile. The seed label or the extension officer can tell you. Also, rotate crops. Do not grow wheat after wheat. Use a legume like faba bean or lentil in between. This breaks disease cycles. Plant on time. Early planting helps avoid rust. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen. Too much nitrogen makes plants soft and prone to disease. Use certified seed. It is clean and disease-free. If you save your own seed, treat it before planting. You can also plant mixtures of varieties. This spreads risk. If one variety fails, others may survive. Always check with your local research station. They test varieties for your area. They can recommend the best ones for drought and disease.

lessons.title: Where to Buy Certified Seed Locally
lessons.body: Certified seed is clean, high-quality seed. It has been inspected and tested. It will give you better yields than saved seed. But where can you buy it? In most African countries, certified seed is sold by licensed agro-dealers. These are shops that sell farm inputs. They are often found in district towns. In Ethiopia, you can buy from the Ethiopian Seed Enterprise (ESE) or from cooperatives. In Kenya, the Kenya Seed Company and Freshco Seeds sell certified wheat and barley. In Tanzania, the Tanzania Seed Company (TANSEED) is a good source. In Nigeria, the National Agricultural Seeds Council (NASC) licenses dealers. You can also buy from research stations. For example, the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) sells seed of new varieties. The Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) also sells seed. Another option is farmer cooperatives. Many cooperatives buy certified seed in bulk and sell to members at a discount. Ask your local extension officer. They know the nearest certified seed dealer. When buying, check the label. It should show the variety name, lot number, germination percentage, and purity. It should also have a certification tag. Do not buy seed from open sacks or without a label. That seed may be fake or poor quality. Also check the date. Seed older than one year may have low germination. Buy from a reputable dealer. Ask other farmers where they buy. Avoid buying from roadside vendors. They often sell uncertified seed. If you cannot find certified seed, you can buy from a trusted farmer who grows certified seed. But you must test it first. Remember, certified seed costs more, but it pays off. It can increase your yield by 20-30%. So invest in good seed.

lessons.title: Testing Seed Germination Before Planting
lessons.body: Before you plant, you must test your seed. Even certified seed can have low germination if it was stored badly. A simple germination test saves you money and time. Here is how to do it. First, collect a sample. Take seeds from different parts of the bag. Mix them together. Then count out 100 seeds. You can use 50 or 20 if you have few seeds. But 100 is easy to calculate. Next, get a clean cloth or paper towel. Moisten it with water. It should be damp, not dripping. Spread the seeds evenly on the cloth. Cover them with another moist cloth. Roll it up. Put the roll in a plastic bag. Keep it in a warm place, around 20-25Â°C. Do not put it in direct sunlight. Check the seeds every day. Keep the cloth moist. After 7 days, count how many seeds have sprouted. A seed is sprouted if the root is at least 1 cm long. The number of sprouted seeds is your germination percentage. For example, if 85 out of 100 seeds sprout, germination is 85%. For wheat and barley, good germination is 85% or higher. If it is 70-85%, you can still plant, but use more seed. If it is below 70%, do not plant it. Buy new seed. You can also do a float test. Put seeds in a glass of water. Good seeds sink. Dead seeds float. Remove the floaters. But this test is not as accurate as the germination test. Another method is the rag-doll test. Use a piece of old cloth. Same steps. Always test before planting. If you store seed, test it again before the next season. Store seed in a cool, dry place. Use airtight containers. Add ash or neem leaves to keep insects away. Never store seed in a damp place. It will rot or germinate too early. With a simple test, you can be sure your seed will grow.

lessons.title: Seed Treatment: Protecting Against Smuts and Bunts
lessons.body: Smuts and bunts are fungal diseases. They attack wheat and barley. They can reduce your yield by 20-50%. The good news is you can prevent them with seed treatment. Seed treatment is coating the seed with a fungicide before planting. This kills the fungus on the seed or in the soil. Common smuts are loose smut, covered smut, and flag smut. Bunts include common bunt and dwarf bunt. These diseases survive in the seed or soil. If you plant untreated seed, the fungus grows with the plant. It produces black spores instead of grain. To treat seed, you need a fungicide. Common ones are carboxin, thiram, and tebuconazole. You can buy them from agro-dealers. They come as powders or liquids. For example, Vitavax and Apron are popular brands. Always read the label. Use the recommended dose. For wheat, a common dose is 2-3 grams of fungicide per kilogram of seed. For barley, use 2 grams per kilogram. You can treat seed in a bucket or a drum. Put the seed in the bucket. Add the fungicide. Mix well with a stick or gloved hands. Make sure every seed is coated. Wear gloves and a mask. Do not eat or drink while treating. After treatment, let the seed dry in the shade. Do not dry in direct sun. Plant within a few days. If you store treated seed, keep it away from food and feed. It is poisonous. Also, do not use treated seed for animal feed or human consumption. Another method is hot water treatment. Soak seed in hot water at 52-54Â°C for 10 minutes. Then cool and dry. This kills loose smut. But it is tricky. You need a thermometer. If water is too hot, it kills the seed. If too cold, it does not kill the fungus. So chemical treatment is safer. Always buy certified seed. It is often already treated. But check the label. If not, treat it yourself. Treating seed is cheap. It costs about $1-2 per 10 kg. It protects your crop. So do not skip this step.

quiz.q: Which wheat class is best for making yeast bread?
quiz.explanation: Bread wheat has high protein and strong gluten, ideal for yeast bread.

quiz.q: What is the main use of durum wheat?
quiz.explanation: Durum wheat is hard and high in protein, used for pasta and couscous.

quiz.q: Which wheat class needs cool, moist conditions?
quiz.explanation: Biscuit wheat yields best in cooler, wetter areas.

quiz.q: How many days does bread wheat typically take to mature?
quiz.explanation: Bread wheat usually matures in 120-150 days.

quiz.q: Which durum wheat variety is grown in Ethiopia?
quiz.explanation: Yerer is a durum wheat variety in Ethiopia.

quiz.q: Two-row barley is known for:
quiz.explanation: Two-row barley has two rows of large, uniform seeds per spike.

quiz.q: Which barley type is mainly used for animal feed?
quiz.explanation: Six-row barley has smaller, less uniform seeds and is mainly used for feed.

quiz.q: Malting barley must have:
options: B) Low protein and high starch
quiz.explanation: Malting barley requires low protein and high starch for good malt quality.

quiz.q: Which African country is a major producer of malting barley?
quiz.explanation: Ethiopia is a major producer of malting barley in Africa.

quiz.q: What is a risk of growing malting barley without a contract?
options: B) No buyer for the grain
D) It is resistant to all diseases
quiz.explanation: Without a contract with a maltster, you may not find a buyer for malting barley.

quiz.q: Which barley variety is two-row?
quiz.explanation: HB-42 is a two-row barley variety.

quiz.q: Drought-tolerant wheat varieties typically:
quiz.explanation: Drought-tolerant varieties often mature early to escape dry spells.

quiz.q: Which wheat variety is drought-tolerant in Ethiopia?
quiz.explanation: Danda'a is a drought-tolerant wheat variety in Ethiopia.

quiz.q: Disease-resistant varieties help against:
quiz.explanation: Disease-resistant varieties are bred to resist fungal diseases like rusts and smuts.

quiz.q: Crop rotation helps control disease by:
quiz.explanation: Rotating crops breaks the life cycle of pathogens that survive in the soil or crop residues.

quiz.q: Which barley variety is resistant to net blotch?
quiz.explanation: HB-42 is resistant to net blotch.

quiz.q: What should you check on a certified seed label?
options: A) Variety name and germination percentage
quiz.explanation: The label should show variety name, lot number, germination percentage, and purity.

quiz.q: Which organization sells certified seed in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: Kenya Seed Company is a major seller of certified seed in Kenya.

quiz.q: Why is certified seed better than saved seed?
options: B) It is disease-free and high quality
quiz.explanation: Certified seed is inspected and tested to be disease-free and of high quality.

quiz.q: What is a good germination percentage for wheat and barley?
quiz.explanation: Good germination for wheat and barley is 85% or higher.

quiz.q: How many seeds should you use for a germination test?
quiz.explanation: Using 100 seeds makes it easy to calculate the germination percentage.

quiz.q: In a germination test, seeds are sprouted after:
quiz.explanation: Most wheat and barley seeds sprout within 7 days under proper conditions.

quiz.q: What does the float test tell you?
quiz.explanation: Good seeds sink, dead seeds float, giving a rough idea of viability.

quiz.q: How should you store seed?
options: C) In a cool, dry place
quiz.explanation: Cool, dry storage keeps seed viable for longer.

quiz.q: What is a common fungicide for seed treatment?
quiz.explanation: Carboxin is a fungicide used for treating seed against smuts and bunts.

quiz.q: What is the recommended dose of fungicide per kg of wheat seed?
quiz.explanation: For wheat, 2-3 grams of fungicide per kilogram of seed is common.

quiz.q: Why should you wear gloves when treating seed?
options: B) To avoid skin contact with poison
quiz.explanation: Fungicides are poisonous, so gloves protect your skin.

quiz.q: Hot water treatment for seed requires water at:
quiz.explanation: Hot water treatment at 52-54Â°C for 10 minutes kills loose smut without killing the seed.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of hot water treatment?
options: B) It is tricky and can damage seed
D) It only works on barley
quiz.explanation: Hot water treatment requires precise temperature control; too hot kills the seed.

quiz.q: Which disease is controlled by seed treatment?
quiz.explanation: Seed treatment is effective against smuts and bunts that live on or in the seed.
